newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria's Balkan airline to renovate its fleet.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria's Balkan airline to renovate its fleet.

text.p: Bulgaria's indebted state carrier Balkan Airlines plans to replace its old Soviet-made planes before the firm is offered for privatisation, Executive Director Valeri Doganov said on Wednesday.

"We are planning to renovate our fleet for the scheduled international routes while we will probably seek...second-hand planes for the charter passenger flights, which are not very profitable," Doganov told a news conference.

The airline has 26 Soviet-made aircraft including Tupolev TU-154s, Ilyushin IL-18s, Antonov AN-12s and AN-24s. It also has two Boeing 767-200s leased from Air France and three Boeing 737-500s leased from Australia's Ansett.

Doganov said he had talked to aircraft producers including Airbus Industrie and Boeing who were prepared to supply new planes. He said Balkan would prefer to buy from one producer to reduce maintenance costs.
He said experts from the companies would visit Bulgaria in the first half of July to make proposals.
Bulgaria plans to sell Balkan next year, and a consultant for the sale is expected to be selected by the end of July. Doganov said 14 firms have already bid for the consultancy.
Balkan, which lost $50 million last year due to leasing fees, the drastic fall of the lev against the dollar and penalties on overdue payments, is operating under a stabilisation programme.
"With the decision of Bulgaria's government, Balkan's domestic debt of $37 million has been reduce. And this way, the company will increase its capital," Doganov said.

He said the company was servicing its foreign debt, worth $60 million at the end of 1996, under a rescheduling plan. The total includes debts to firms for fuel supplies and unpaid taxes for flights over other countries.

In the first five months of 1997, the airline cut total losses by 40 percent against year ago levels, Doganov said, adding that the company's loss from flying operations had been reduced to $5.3 million from $8.8 million.
Balkan's income in the first five months of 1997 from charter and regular passenger flights was $905,000 against a loss of $1.3 million in the same period last year.
Income from cargo charter and regular flights in the first five months was $751,000 compared to a $1.1 million loss in the same 1996 period.
Balkan will sell some of its real estate abroad, which includes apartments and offices, Doganov said.
Balkan wants to sell its Pliska hotel here, but the Privatisation Agency blocked the sale at the request of Bulgaria's Economic Bank because Balkan owes the bank $11 million.
Japanese firm Orix Corp is seeking $11.5 million from Balkan, which returned four Airbus A320s leased from the firm and terminated its contract at the end of 1996, he said.
Orix is seeking $5.7 million for technical restoration of the leased planes and another $5.8 million for leasing taxes.
Doganov said the agreement signed by Balkan's previous management for terminating the contract was not favourable.
"We may go to court, but we will seek a favourable decision for both sides," he said.
